This 72-year-old male presents with classic signs and laboratory/imaging findings of *painless, obstructive (cholestatic) jaundice*: jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, pale stools, elevated direct bilirubin (>85%), markedly elevated ALP, and preserved transaminases (AST/ALT normal). The ultrasound shows biliary ductal dilation *plus* an anechoic cystic subhepatic mass — highly consistent with a distended, non-inflamed gallbladder (Courvoisier’s sign), which strongly argues against chronic stone disease (e.g., choledocholithiasis) and instead points to *malignant distal biliary obstruction*. The presence of significant unintentional weight loss (6.3 kg in 2 weeks) and age >70 further elevate malignancy probability. While cholangiocarcinoma (perihilar or distal) and ampullary carcinoma are in the differential, pancreatic head cancer is the *most common cause* of painless jaundice with Courvoisier’s sign and weight loss in this demographic. Benign causes (e.g., autoimmune pancreatitis, strictures) are less likely given the absence of pain, normal IgG4 (not measured but not suggested), and lack of inflammatory or autoimmune features in labs/imaging. The preserved liver enzymes rule out primary hepatocellular disease; the pattern is purely obstructive.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Painless jaundice in a 72-year-old male  
- Pruritus, dark urine, and pale stools — classic cholestatic symptoms  
- Total bilirubin 5.6 mg/dL with direct fraction 4.8 mg/dL (>85% conjugated)  
- ALP elevated (192 U/L) with normal AST (32 U/L) and ALT (34 U/L) → isolated cholestatic pattern  
- Ultrasound shows dilation of both intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts  
- Ultrasound reveals an anechoic cystic mass in the subhepatic region — consistent with Courvoisier’s gallbladder  
- Significant unintentional weight loss (6.3 kg) over 2 weeks  
- History of long-term alcohol use (though abstinent for 3 years — makes alcoholic hepatitis/chronic cirrhosis unlikely as cause of current jaundice)  
- No reported abdominal pain — argues against biliary colic or acute cholecystitis  

[GAPS]  
- CA 19-9 level (not yet obtained; would support pancreatic/cholangiocarcinoma if elevated, though false negatives occur in Lewis-negative individuals)  
- MRCP or contrast-enhanced CT findings (to localize obstruction site and identify a pancreatic head mass or stricture)  
- IgG4 level (to exclude IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis or autoimmune pancreatitis)  
- Liver biopsy or cytology (e.g., ERCP brushings or FNA) — not yet performed  
- Histopathologic confirmation — absent  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma
